entries.title: Designing for sovereign AI: A shared foundation from edge to cloud
entries.summary: A flexible sovereign architecture allows organizations to place each workload in the right environment, apply the controls it requires, and maintain consistency. The post Designing for sovereign AI: A shared foundation from edge to cloud appeared first on Microsoft Azure Blog.
entries.content:
As organizations apply AI to more business-critical and data-intensive workloads, AI processing is moving closer to where data is created, decisions are made, and operations take place.

  • Manufacturers can analyze confidential production data next to the systems that generate it.
  • Pharmaceutical companies can apply AI to clinical trials within controlled environments.
  • Government agencies can run AI applications on sensitive information while maintaining established security and operational boundaries.

This shift reflects ongoing innovation across the technology ecosystem to give organizations greater flexibility in where they run AI and process sensitive data, and it is changing the digital sovereignty conversation. It now encompasses where data is stored and processed, where workloads run, who can access and operate the systems around them, and how those systems remain secure and operational as requirements change. The next phase of digital sovereignty will take shape across the technology ecosystem, through closer alignment among silicon, infrastructure, cloud, security, data, and AI.

As AI extends into more sensitive and mission-critical workloads, sovereignty must be designed across the stack, from silicon and infrastructure to cloud, data, and AI. Microsoft and Intel® are working together to help organizations create a more consistent foundation for innovation, while retaining greater choice over where workloads run and how they are controlled.

A flexible sovereign architecture allows organizations to place each workload in the right environment, apply the controls it requires, and maintain a more consistent technology and operating foundation as requirements evolve.

Sovereignty must work across the technology stack

Sovereignty requirements vary by workload. The right level of control depends on factors such as data sensitivity, regulation, latency, connectivity, operational access, and resilience requirements. This creates a continuum, where organizations can apply different levels of control across public cloud, customer-controlled environments, and trusted partner solutions.

Delivering that flexibility requires the underlying technology layers to work together. The controls that shape where a workload runs, how data is protected, who can access it, and how the environment is verified extend across silicon, infrastructure, cloud, security, data, and AI.

This is where the Microsoft and Intel partnership comes into focus. Together, we are working to create a more consistent foundation across these layers, giving organizations greater choice in where workloads run and how they are controlled. This principle is central to the work between Microsoft and Intel. Azure Local, running on Intel® Xeon® 6 processors, brings distributed Azure infrastructure together with a common compute foundation for customer-controlled environments. Organizations can extend cloud and AI capabilities closer to their data and operations while maintaining consistent approaches to security, management, and governance.

Trust must be designed for and verified

For sensitive workloads, trust must be supported by technical protections and verifiable evidence. Organizations need to protect workloads across the technology stack and verify that systems are operating under the security conditions they have established.

That starts at the compute layer and extends through identity, encryption, governance, policy, and operations. For supported Azure Confidential VM configurations, Intel® Xeon® processors provide hardware-based protections, including Intel® Trust Domain Extensions (Intel TDX), which can help isolate workloads while they are in use. Hardware-backed attestation can provide evidence that helps organizations verify relevant security properties of the environment against their requirements. Microsoft extends this foundation through security and governance controls across cloud and customer-controlled environments.

Together, these capabilities can help organizations verify relevant security properties of the environment against their requirements. This is particularly important as AI brings regulated, proprietary, and mission-critical data into new workloads.

Each workload should receive protections proportionate to its risk. Isolation, encryption, attestation, and operational controls can be applied where they provide meaningful value while preserving a manageable operating model across the broader environment.

Digital sovereignty requires trust across the technology stack. Together, Intel and Microsoft are combining hardware-based security and confidential computing with cloud, AI and distributed infrastructure to help customers protect sensitive workloads and verify the environments in which they run. This shared foundation gives organizations greater control, confidence and choice, with the performance and scale to continue innovating as AI moves into more regulated and mission-critical environments.

—Anand Pashupathy, Vice President and General Manager, Intel Product Assurance and Security

Sovereign AI brings intelligence closer to data

Much of the data with the greatest potential for AI must remain within defined operational, regulatory, or security boundaries. This includes data tied to industrial operations, government services, clinical environments, intellectual property, and proprietary research.

Workload placement has therefore become a practical AI decision. Organizations need the flexibility to run AI closer to their data, applications, and operations. Delivering that flexibility requires infrastructure, cloud platforms, AI software, and security capabilities to work as a connected foundation.

Microsoft Foundry helps organizations build and deploy AI applications and models, with options for where AI runs based on their requirements. Foundry Local enables organizations to run AI inference in their own environments, closer to the data and applications those models rely on. On the same infrastructure, Intel Xeon 6 processors with Intel® Advanced Matrix Extensions (Intel AMX) can accelerate AI workloads directly on the CPU. Intel® OpenVINO™ helps developers optimize and deploy models across supported infrastructure.

This approach extends across the broader application environment. Organizations may need to manage AI, applications, data, development, and productivity workloads within the same governance and operational boundary. Microsoft 365 Local and GitHub Enterprise Local extend customer-controlled options to collaboration, source code, and software development workflows.

Sovereign AI brings models, data, applications, development tools, and infrastructure together under the controls each workload requires. This approach allows organizations to apply AI within the operational and governance boundaries established for their most sensitive data.

Organizations want to apply AI to their most valuable data while maintaining the controls that data requires. On supported Azure confidential VM configurations, Intel TDX helps make that possible by running AI workloads in hardware-isolated trust domains, protecting models and data while in use and isolating them from the host and hypervisor. Hardware-backed attestation then gives organizations evidence they can check against their own requirements, so they can move from trusting their environment to verifying it.

—Anand Pashupathy, Vice President and General Manager, Intel Product Assurance and Security

Sovereignty architecture must be adaptable

Sovereignty requirements will continue to change. A workload that runs in a connected environment today may face different regulatory, resilience, or connectivity requirements tomorrow. AI models, applications, and infrastructure will also continue to evolve.

A sovereign architecture must therefore provide control without creating rigidity. Organizations should be able to adapt where workloads run, how they are secured, and how they connect without rebuilding their management and security model each time requirements change.

This is another reason partnership across the technology stack matters. Alignment across silicon, infrastructure, cloud, security, and AI software can give organizations a more stable foundation even as individual technologies and workload requirements evolve.

A well-designed sovereign architecture gives organizations room to respond as regulations, technologies, and operating conditions change.

Explore Microsoft Sovereign Cloud in Europe

Discover how Microsoft Sovereign Cloud in Europe helps organizations address evolving data sovereignty, security, and compliance requirements while accelerating cloud and AI innovation.

Three questions leaders should ask

Digital sovereignty can become abstract quickly. A better place to start is the workload.

1. What must remain under your control?

Consider the data, infrastructure, administrative access, software operations, and connectivity on which the workload depends. The answer may differ by application, even within the same organization.

2. Can you verify that those controls are working?

Policies and contractual commitments are important, but sensitive workloads may also require technical evidence. Consider how your architecture supports encryption, isolation, identity and access control, policy enforcement, attestation, and operational transparency.

3. Will the architecture leave you room to adapt?

AI capabilities, regulations, operating conditions, and workload requirements will continue to change. Your architecture should allow you to adopt new models, move processing closer to data, and adjust where workloads run without creating an entirely separate technology environment each time.

Digital sovereignty depends on cloud, infrastructure, security, AI, and silicon working together. Our collaboration with Intel gives customers a more consistent foundation across these layers, so they can apply stronger controls where needed while retaining the flexibility to innovate.

—Bernardo Caldas, CVP, Azure Edge Product Management

The strongest sovereignty strategy preserves choice

Digital sovereignty should give organizations greater control over the technology and data they depend on while preserving their capacity to innovate.

Achieving that outcome requires collaboration across the technology ecosystem. Microsoft and Intel are connecting silicon, infrastructure, cloud, security, and AI to give organizations greater flexibility in where workloads run, how they are protected, and how they evolve.

A strong sovereignty strategy meets today’s requirements while preserving tomorrow’s options.

Resources to learn more

  • Dive deeper into digital sovereignty to learn how Microsoft is helping organizations address data residency, operational control, security, and regulatory requirements across cloud and customer-controlled environments.
  • Learn more about Microsoft Sovereign Private Cloud.
  • Join us at Microsoft Ignite in November to hear the latest on Microsoft Sovereign Cloud, Azure Local, AI, security, and infrastructure innovation.

entries.title: Managing open-weight model risk in enterprise deployments
entries.summary: The growing AI landscape is giving enterprises more choice in how they build, customize, and deploy increasingly capable models. The post Managing open-weight model risk in enterprise deployments appeared first on Microsoft Azure Blog.
entries.content:
The growing AI landscape is giving enterprises more choice in how they build, customize, and deploy increasingly capable models. Open-weight models are an important part of that landscape. They give enterprises access to model weights and greater flexibility to inspect, evaluate, modify, and run models within their own environments.

While that flexibility can be valuable, it also affects how enterprises evaluate models, where they implement safeguards, and who is responsible for maintaining those safeguards over time.

As enterprises choose which models to deploy, the relevant question is broader than whether a model is open-weight or closed-weight. Enterprises need to understand what they are using the model for, what could go wrong in that context, and what evidence and controls they need to manage risks.

Today, Microsoft and NVIDIA are publishing Risk Management for Open-Weight Models in Enterprise, the first in a planned series of joint resources intended to help enterprises address those questions. The paper introduces a shared risk taxonomy and an approach to managing model risks grounded in established standards and frameworks, including International Organization for Standardization (ISO) standards and the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) AI Risk Management Framework.

The paper reflects a core idea: weight openness alone does not determine an AI system’s risk. Risk depends on the model, use case, deployment, and safeguards.

Read the whitepaper: Risk Management for Open-Weight Models in Enterprise

Understanding risk in the deployment context

Open- and closed-weight models can share many of the same underlying risks, but how those risks materialize depends on the deployment. A model used to help an employee draft a document presents different considerations than the same model used in a customer-facing workflow, just as a standalone inference endpoint differs from a system connected to external data or tools.

The architecture matters too. A risk may originate in the model, while the most effective control may sit in the inference environment, application, or surrounding operational processes. The joint guidance looks beyond the model label to factors including provenance, intended use, users, deployment conditions, and surrounding controls. This first paper focuses primarily on model-layer risks. Evaluating a model alone does not establish the safety of an agent or application: teams must also assess its permissions, data access, tools, runtime, and operational controls.

Establishing a common language

Managing these risks consistently also requires a common vocabulary across engineering, security, legal, safety, and business teams.

The initial Microsoft and NVIDIA taxonomy organizes risks into five broad categories: Cybersecurity, Data Protection, Content, Human-AI Interaction, and Bias. It is not a policy or deployment checklist, but instead it should be used by enterprises to adapt it to their own systems, use cases, and risk criteria, then connect relevant risks to evaluations, mitigations, and accountable owners.

Using evaluations as risk evidence

Evaluations help turn the taxonomy into something enterprises can use. The paper maps evaluations to a selection of risks across the five categories, giving teams a way to start with a risk that matters for their deployment and identify evaluations that can produce relevant evidence about it.

Microsoft Foundry helps enterprises assess quality, groundedness, and safety with built-in and custom evaluations and automated red teaming. Its configurable content-safety controls help detect and mitigate harmful inputs and outputs and prompt attacks. Teams should validate control availability for their model and deployment, including preview status, and combine these capabilities with application-specific testing, monitoring, and human oversight.

Evaluations still need to be interpreted in the context of a particular deployment and the goal is to make it easier for teams to connect the risks they identify with useful evidence, while building a broader set of evaluation resources that can evolve alongside models, deployment patterns, and emerging risks. Microsoft and NVIDIA plan to use the joint repository to share additional evaluations and point to existing resources that can help enterprises assess specific risks.

Accounting for changes in control and responsibility

Open-weight access gives enterprises greater control over how a model is evaluated, modified, and deployed. Model access and deployment are separate choices: open-weight models can also be used through managed platforms. Responsibility for safeguards depends on the service and deployment configuration; enterprises that operate their own model deployments may take on controls otherwise provided by a managed service.

Those safeguards can operate at different layers, and (depending on the risk) enterprises might use model changes, access controls, input and output filtering, monitoring, or human review. The important step is connecting each identified risk to controls that can effectively address it within the deployed system. Those decisions need to be revisited as models and deployments change.

Building on this work

Risk Management for Open-Weight Models in Enterprise focuses primarily on the model layer. Future work from Microsoft and NVIDIA is intended to extend this approach across the runtime, harness, and application layers, with additional technical guidance on evaluation and mitigation.

We also expect the resources supporting this work to evolve as new models, evaluations, and deployment patterns emerge. The joint repository will provide a place to share additional evaluation resources, including contributions from the broader community.

For enterprises deploying open-weight models today, the paper provides guidance they can begin applying to their own use cases. We encourage developers, security practitioners, researchers, and others working in this space to read the paper, explore the evaluations, and contribute evaluations that can help strengthen this shared body of work.

Read the joint Microsoft-NVIDIA paper, Risk Management for Open-Weight Models in Enterprise.

Explore the joint repository and technical resources.

Risk Management for Open-Weight Models in Enterprise was developed jointly by Microsoft and NVIDIA, with Andrew Berkley and April Chen of Microsoft and Michael Boone, Eileen Long, and Arun Rao of NVIDIA leading the development and editing of the paper.

Explore Microsoft Foundry evaluations and content-safety controls for implementation guidance.

entries.title: Evolving the cloud-native foundation for the next generation of AI
entries.summary: Discover how Azure is advancing cloud-native infrastructure to help organizations build, run, and optimize applications and agents at scale. The post Evolving the cloud-native foundation for the next generation of AI appeared first on Microsoft Azure Blog.
entries.content:
Building a cloud-native foundation for AI

The relationship between model innovation and AI infrastructure has never been more clear; as AI becomes more capable, the platform underneath it matters even more. Agents are fundamentally changing how applications work, and with that, what organizations need from the cloud.

Cloud-native practices gave organizations the scale, flexibility and resilience to build a generation of distributed applications. Agents build on that foundation, but they work differently, placing new demands on it. Unlike applications designed around more predictable workflows, agents behave in entirely new ways, gathering information and deep intelligence from across the business, using tools, making decisions, and coordinating work across long-running processes. To complete complex tasks, they pause for approval, respond to new information in real time and change course as conditions evolve. All this changes what the platform needs to deliver.

Customers need infrastructure that adapts as demand changes, applications that remain reliable as work becomes more dynamic, and the visibility and control to understand what is happening across the system. Meeting those needs doesn’t mean starting over, but it does require that the cloud-native foundation organizations already rely on, to evolve. Compute, storage and networking need to work together. Application platforms need to make it easier to build and run AI workloads. Open technologies need to give customers flexibility without adding unnecessary complexity.

The platform decisions organizations make today are increasingly strategic, shaping how effectively they can put AI to work for their business. Evolving the cloud-native foundation is essential to helping organizations get more from AI today while giving them the flexibility to take advantage of new capabilities as they emerge.

Optimize infrastructure for AI workloads

The true measure of AI infrastructure is the useful work it enables. AI workloads rarely place the same demands on infrastructure from beginning to end. Different parts of the work may need accelerated compute, CPUs, fast access to data or connectivity across applications and environments. The answer isn’t simply more capacity, but rather, to match the right resources to the right work at the right time.

That makes coordination across the infrastructure extremely important. Compute, storage and networking need to work together as demands change. When they do, teams can spend less time managing infrastructure and more time focused on the applications and outcomes that matter to their business.

Economics matter, too. Infrastructure needs to be tuned to the demands of the application and the business value it delivers, with the right balance of performance, reliability and cost across the complete workload.

Basecamp Research is one example. The company used Azure to assemble 9.7 trillion nucleotides for EDEN, its therapeutic-design models, and reported laboratory validation across three therapeutic applications within about three weeks. In this example, AI didn’t simply require more infrastructure, it needed AI infrastructure that was coordinated and designed around the outcome – bringing together the compute, data and platform capabilities needed to move complex work forward.

As Glen Gowers, co-founder of Basecamp Research put it: “To really be successful here, we need those three ingredients to come together. We need someone scaling the data; that’s us. But someone who really knows how to scale models and scale compute is Microsoft.”

Leadership takeaway: Measure success by the useful work AI completes. Judge infrastructure investment by the performance, reliability and cost of delivering those outcomes, with compute, storage and networking operating as one system.

Turn open-source innovation into production capability

Open technologies have long helped drive cloud innovation, and AI is accelerating that pace. New models, frameworks and cloud-native technologies give organizations more choice in how they build and adapt applications.

That opportunity builds on an established cloud-native foundation. Gartner forecasts that by 2028, 95% of new AI agent deployment will use Kubernetes.1 Reusing established components can shorten the path to production, allowing developers to focus on differentiated business capabilities rather than rebuilding the foundation.

More choice can also bring more complexity. Taking advantage of open-source innovation often requires specialized expertise to integrate, manage and maintain technologies in production. That expertise is hard to find and even harder to scale. We need to make these capabilities accessible to more businesses, without requiring every organization to build and maintain that expertise themselves.

Azure helps reduce that burden. Services like Azure Kubernetes Service give teams access to open-source innovation while helping manage the complexity and risk of running it in production. This makes it easier for more businesses to take advantage of open technologies while preserving the flexibility to adapt with changing needs.

Leadership takeaway: Choose a platform that helps turn open-source freedom into business advantage. Preserve the ability to adapt and optimize while reducing the expertise and operating effort required to sustain those choices in production.

Align AI infrastructure costs with business value

As more organizations put AI into production, understanding the economics becomes increasingly important. AI investment starts with an expectation of business value: faster decisions, more responsive services or greater capacity to get useful work done. Then, it’s evaluating whether the value justifies the investment to deliver it. FinOps can help teams understand that return and make more informed decisions in this area.

For customers, that starts with understanding the full investment required to run AI applications and how to optimize it as workloads scale. Models represent a significant expense, with token usage and agent behavior influencing spending. Compute, storage, networking and operations also factor into the equation. Considering these together helps customers make more informed decisions about where to optimize.

Teams can’t simply place their bets on spending less. They need to carefully consider that a more capable model or additional infrastructure that costs more may be the right choice if it produces greater value long-term. Teams need to understand the full cost, establish ownership and put guardrails in place as they scale. From there, they can use business outcomes to decide where to optimize and where to invest.

Leadership takeaway: Manage AI investment against the business return it needs to deliver. Evaluate model and platform costs together, then use evidence of outcome value to decide where to optimize and where to invest.

Transform cloud operations with agentic AI

Operations teams are already stretched thin, keeping critical services running while balancing competing priorities and constant change. AI adds new complexity, and it also creates an opportunity to change how those environments are managed.

Cloud-native operations gave teams a new model for managing infrastructure, bringing increased automation, visibility and resilience. Agentic operations build on that foundation, bringing deeper intelligence across applications and infrastructure by connecting signals from otherwise disconnected systems. This helps teams identify issues earlier and resolve them faster, while increasing automation and continuously improving how their environments perform; all within the tools they already use.

Over time, AI can help operations teams move from reacting to problems toward anticipating and addressing them before they disrupt the business. As these capabilities mature, more actions can be automated within defined controls, with people remaining in the loop and accountable for critical decisions. When operations teams have greater reach without additional manual effort, reliability, performance and cost are continuously improved while critical services remain uninterrupted.

Leadership takeaway: Invest in operations that can anticipate problems and coordinate action across the environment. Expand autonomy as capabilities are validated, with clear controls and human accountability protecting critical business services.

Build a cloud-native AI foundation on Azure

Azure serves as the foundation customers need to put AI to work at scale. That means infrastructure designed around the complete workload, access to open innovation without unnecessary complexity, and a clear view of cost and business value. Greater intelligence across cloud operations helps teams anticipate issues and continuously improve how their environments perform as application needs evolve.

We’re continuing to invest in capabilities across Azure that give customers greater flexibility in how they build and run AI applications. From secure, isolated environments for agents to simpler application deployment and the ability to run workloads across cloud and edge environments, these investments help customers take advantage of new capabilities without adding unnecessary operational complexity.

AI is changing what applications can do, and Azure has already evolved to support that shift. The cloud platform has to evolve with them. Years of focused engineering investment have built the foundation for some of the most advanced AI workloads running today, with continued innovation to support what comes next.

Build for the next generation of AI

Platform value compounds when improvements reinforce one another: faster information access keeps compute productive, operational insight exposes waste, and open technologies preserve room to adapt. The leadership task is to make those gains work together. That is the next chapter of cloud native: a foundation that turns advances in AI into dependable business value.

To learn more about the recent Azure innovations and how Azure is evolving the cloud-native foundation for AI applications and agents, explore:

Explore what this means for your organization. Register for our upcoming discovery session to learn how to put a cloud-native foundation for AI applications and agents into practice.
